p.seg: it is not something that inferior scholars can hear,
how can shallow knowledge fathom it!
The "Zi" (Master) that is spoken of,
is a respectful title for those who have virtue,
in ancient times, teachers were called "Zi".
It is also said that "Zi" is the title of the book,
not just the collective name for three sections,
but also a common title for the hundred schools of thought.
As for what is meant by "Inner Chapters,"
"Inner" is named in relation to "Outer," to establish a distinction.
"Chapter" (篇) means a collection of bamboo slips arranged together.
In ancient times, they scraped bamboo to make slips,
and used leather to bind them.
Arranging the slips creates a chapter,
just as connecting sheets of paper today creates a scroll.
Therefore, Yuan Kai said:
"Important matters are recorded on bamboo tablets,
while minor matters are recorded on simple slips."
"Inner" discusses fundamental principles,
while "Outer" speaks of events and traces.
Though events are clearly visible,
they cannot be understood without principle;
though principles are profound and subtle,
they cannot be revealed without events.
Wanting to first clarify the subtle principles,
therefore, we first present the Inner Chapters.
The Inner Chapters contain profound principles,
therefore, we separately establish the titles of each chapter outside the main text.
Guō Xiàng 郭象 still annotated directly beneath the titles,
such as "Xiāoyáo" 逍遙 and "Qíwù" 齊物.
From the outer chapters onwards,
he took the first two characters of the chapter to be its title,
such as "Piánmǔ" 駢拇 and "Mǎtí" 馬蹄.

Preface to Zhuāngzǐ
Written by Guō Xiàng Zǐxuán of Hénán
Now, Zhuāngzǐ,
can be said to have understood the root.
Therefore, he never concealed his wild words,
words that, though not calculated, are uniquely responsive.
Now, to be responsive without calculation,
is to be useless even if correct.
If words do not concern material affairs,
they cannot be put into practice, no matter how lofty.
This is quite different from being silent and still,
and only arising when absolutely necessary.
There is indeed a separation,
this can be said to be knowing the one who has no mind.
For the mind is without action,
then it responds to feelings as they arise,
responding according to the time,
words are only careful.
Therefore, it becomes one with transformation,
flowing through ten thousand generations and merging with things,
how could it have ever set up opposition, uniquely encountered, and engaged in idle talk beyond the realm?
This is why it is unconventional and yet the crown of all schools of thought.
However, although Zhuāng Shēng did not embody it,
his words reached its height.
He understood the principle of heaven and earth,
explained the nature of all things,
comprehended the changes of life and death,
and clarified the Way of the Inner Sage and Outer King,
above he knew that the Creator is without things,
below he knew that the existence of things is self-created.
His words are broad and generous,
his meaning is profound and subtle.
The ultimate of the Ultimate Way,
blends subtle meanings with elegance;
serenely releasing and letting go,
letting go without arrogance.
Therefore, it is said he did not know where righteousness should go,
wildly and recklessly walked and trod on its great principle;
holding food in the mouth and rejoicing in serenity,
patting the belly and wandering in chaos (one).
The ultimate (man) [benevolent man] reaches the point of being without attachment,
filial piety and kindness eventually lead to complete forgetting,
rituals and music return to what one is already capable of,
loyalty and trustworthiness emanate from the light of heaven.
By using that light, simplicity naturally forms itself.
Therefore, the divine instrument transforms uniquely in the realm of the mysterious and dark, and its source and flow are deep and long (three).
Thus, what its long waves wash away,
what its high winds fan,
thoroughly suits the appropriateness of things,
and fits the desires of the people.
Broaden their narrowness,
resolve their doubts,
even without the application of purifying effort,
the grounds for pride and boasting dissipate.
Therefore, reading his book,
one surpassingly feels that he has already attained,
passing through Kunlun,
traversing the great void,
and wandering in the courts of elusiveness.
Even avaricious people,
impetuous scholars,
if they but briefly grasp its lingering fragrance,
taste its overflowing current,
and vaguely perceive its sounds and shadows,
are still sufficiently enlightened to have a feeling of forgetting their form and attaining self-satisfaction.
How much more so for those who explore its distant meaning and savor eternal life!
Thus, one extends far into the clear distance,
leaves behind the dust of the world, and returns to the ultimate darkness.
【Corrections】 (One) The character "芒" (máng, awn) in the Song dynasty Zhao Jianyi version is written as "茫" (máng, vast).
(Two) The character "仁" (rén, benevolence) is corrected according to the ancient Yi Congshu reprint of the Song version.
(Three) "源流深長" (yuánliú shēn cháng, the source is deep and the flow is long) in the Zhao Jianyi version is written as "源深流長" (yuán shēn liú cháng, the source is deep, the flow is long).
Preface to Zhuangzi
Written by Cheng Xuanying, a Tang Dynasty West Hua Dharma Master
Now, Zhuangzi,
is what explains the deep root of morality,
narrates the wondrous essence of profound mystery,
expresses the tranquility of non-action,
illuminates the obscurity of solitary transformation,
restrains the nine schools,
encompasses the hundred schools,
truly is the supreme teaching within the region,
indeed, it is the subtle words beyond phenomena.
The person's surname is Zhuang,
given name Zhou,
courtesy name Zixiu,
born in Meng County, Suiyang, Song State,
studied under Master Changsang,
received the title "Immortal of South Hua".
At the beginning of the Warring States period,
at the end of the declining Zhou dynasty,
lamenting the meager achievements of the people,
grieving the decline of morality,
he thus bravely rose in indignation,
and consequently wrote this treatise.
Its words are vast and broad,
its essence is deep and far-reaching,
has been explained differently throughout ancient and modern times.
Now, I will broadly outline the main points
and briefly offer three interpretations.
These three interpretations are:
First,
Gù Tóngbǎi 顧桐柏 said:
"Xiāo 逍 means
to dissolve;
yáo 遙 means
distant.
Dissolving completely the burden of deliberate action,
and seeing distantly the principle of non-action.
To wander in this way,
is why it is called 'Xiāoyáo.'"
Second,
Zhī Dàolín 支道林 said:
"Managing all things without being managed by them,
therefore one is carefree and doesn't rely on oneself;
profound insight is not hurried yet swift,
therefore one is free and there is nothing one does not do.
Wandering the world in this way,
is why it is called 'Xiāoyáo Yóu.'"
Third,
Mù Yèyún 穆夜云 said:
"Xiāoyáo 逍遙 is
essentially a name for unrestrained and self-satisfied attainment.
When perfect virtue fills one from within,
there is no time that is not suitable;
Therefore, one can achieve great equality among myriad realms.
Therefore, "On the Equality of Things" follows.
Having pointed out the hoof of a horse (as one with) Heaven and Earth,
and merging with the myriad things,
with a spirit of tranquil serenity,
one can nurture and safeguard life.
Therefore, "The Principle of Nurturing Life" follows.
Having forgotten both good and evil,
and both realms and wisdom are exquisitely subtle,
following changes and yielding to transformations,
one can live and interact within the human world.
Therefore, "The Human World" follows.
Inner virtue is complete,
therefore one can disperse one's virtue,
externally to connect with things.
And then, following the rising and falling of things,
inner and outer (realities) are in silent accord.
Therefore, "Signs of Perfect Virtue" follows.
Still water is a flowing mirror,
connecting with things without intention,
forgetting virtue and forgetting form,
in accord with the ultimate of meeting the outer and uniting with the inner.
One can craft and form the myriad things.
Therefore, "The Great and Venerable Teacher" follows.
The true sages of old,
understood Heaven and understood humanity,
shared the same function as creation,
being both still and responsive.
Thereafter, he drove and directed the myriad things,
therefore, he followed up with "Responding to Emperors and Kings."
"Webbed Fingers" and following chapters,
all take the first two characters of the chapter as the title,
and have no other meaning,
so I will not discuss those chapters again.
But from ancient times, noble scholars,
recluses of the Jin and Han dynasties,
all never failed to admire and study it,
and to create explanations for it;
although there are no flaws in the commentaries and explanations,
and there are beautiful words,
all are able to seek out the hidden meanings.
Xuán Yīng, disregarding his own ordinariness and dullness,
learned it from a young age,
and has been diligently studying and deeply contemplating it for thirty years.
Based on the thirty chapters commented on by Zǐ Xuán,
he has thus written a commentary,
totaling thirty scrolls.
Although the wording is clumsy and unskilled,
it still has somewhat of a direction and destination for the heart and mind;
I dare not leave it to later generations,
but simply record it for my own remembrance of what I might forget.
【Correction】 (1) The character "蹄" (tí, hoof) is also erroneously added in the replicated Song edition,
according to the meaning of the "Equality of Things" chapter, "Heaven and earth are one finger,
all things are one horse," it should be deleted.
Preface to the Collected Interpretations of Zhuangzi
Guō Jūnzǐ completed the Collected Interpretations of Zhuangzi,
And gave it to Xiānqiān to read,
and that year happened to have the Dongyi rebellion,
and (he) rose and sighed, saying:
Zhuāngzǐ must have had some compelling reason in his heart!
For he encountered a world of blockage and obstruction,
and there was no way to salvage it,
his spirit wandered in the vastness,
examining the boundlessness of small and large,
investigating the beginning and end of heaven and earth,
and in fear made these words.
Zōu Yǎn said:
"What the Confucians call the Middle Kingdom,
in the world is only one of eighty-one parts.
Outside the Red County Divine Province, there are nine continents,
surrounded by a coastal sea,
and the great ocean surrounds them."
Huì Shī said:
"I know the center of the world,
it is north of Yān,
and south of Yuè."
And Zhuāngzǐ praised them,
and also spoke of Shū and Hū drilling the chaos to death,
his words seem to foresee the future and infer its ultimate end,
truly a different person!
Zǐgòng made a shadoof for drawing water,
and the old man of Hànyīn laughed at him.
Today's mechanical devices and contraptions,
are ten thousand times greater than the shadoof.
If you were to have Zhuangzi see this,
what would he say?
The Mán and Chù clans fight over territory on a snail's horn,
resulting in tens of thousands of corpses,
chasing the defeated for ten days.
The Mán and Chù clans of today are countless in number,
so what could Zhuangzi do?
Therefore, even with the Yellow Emperor as ruler, there was Chiyou,
and with Yao as ruler, there were Congzhi, Zong, Kuai, and Xu Ao.
The Yellow Emperor and Yao were not fond of such affairs,
yet they wanted to empty their state
and punish their people.
It was decisively clear
that they could not govern with emptiness and stillness.
That Zhuangzi,
seeking his methods but failing to find them,
will then go on to live alone in the vast wilderness,
hoping to preserve his life and enjoy his existence,
how can he possibly concern himself with the world!
Moreover, his writings have long been exposed to later generations.
The Jin dynasty developed them into metaphysics,
which offered no solution to the chaos of the barbarian Hu and Jie tribes;
the Tang dynasty revered them as true scriptures,
which provided no salvation from the An Lushan Rebellion.
They merely serve to intoxicate rulers with indulgence and extravagance,
and dilute the common people's pursuit of profit and desire,
perhaps offering a slight bit of help in one or two instances.
And his writing is exceptionally remarkable,
Guō Jūn loved playing with it endlessly,
thus, he had a compilation and interpretation made,
appending it with prose,
enriching it with broad knowledge.
If Zhuāngzǐ saw it,
wouldn't he say, "This is just my dregs and leavings"?
However,
without footprints, how can one measure the shoe,
without dregs and leavings, how can one observe the ancient beauty!
Therefore, Master Guō wrote this book to be a subsidiary to ink,
intending that all under heaven become descendants who recite it in the style of Luò!
In the twelfth month of winter, in the year Jiǎwǔ, the twentieth year of Guangxu (光緒),
respectfully written by your foolish younger brother from Chángshā, Wáng Xiānqiān.

◎ Qìngfān notes, Liú Yìqìng's *Shìshuō Xīnyǔ*, Literary category, says:
"Zhuāngzǐ's Free and Easy Wandering chapter,
was formerly a difficult point;
something that the various famous worthies could delve into,
but could not extract a principle beyond that of Guō Xiàng.
Zhī Dàolín, at the White Horse Temple,
was conversing with Féng Tàicháng,
and the discussion reached carefree wandering.
Zhī strikingly marked out a new principle beyond the two families,
establishing a different meaning beyond the various worthies,
all of which were things the various famous worthies sought to understand but could not,
and later they adopted Zhī's principle."
Liú Xiàobiāo's commentary says:
"Xiàng Zǐqī and Guō Zǐxuán's explanation of carefree wandering says:
'The great Peng bird soars to ninety thousand *lǐ*,
while the little sparrow rises to the elm and sandalwood trees;
although the small and great differ,
each fulfills its nature.
If each is fulfilling their lot,
that is also carefree wandering.
However, the myriad things,
all rely on something to depend on.
Only by obtaining what they depend on,
can they then be carefree.
Only the sage merges with things and follows the great changes,
Is able to be without reliance and constantly connected.
How could it be merely self-connected!
Moreover, those who depend on something do not lose what they depend on,
not losing it is equivalent to great connection."
Zhī's Discussion on Untrammeled Wandering says:
"Now, untrammeled wandering,
illuminates the mind of the perfect person.
Zhuāng Shēng established words on the Great Dao,
and metaphorically referred to the *peng* bird and the sparrow.
The *peng* bird, because its path of survival is vast,
therefore loses comfort to things external to itself;
the sparrow, because it is near and laughs at the distance,
has self-importance and boasting within its mind.
The perfect person rides the heavenly correctness and enjoys high spirits,
wandering endlessly in abandonment.
He deals with things, but is not dealt with by things,
and thus wanders freely, not finding himself constrained;
his profound response is non-doing,
not quick but swift,
and thus he wanders freely, not failing to be comfortable.
This is the reason for being untrammeled and free.
As for having desires that meet their fulfillment,
fulfilled in what is fulfilled,
happily resembling innate nature,
it is like a hungry person having one full meal,
a thirsty person having one full drink.
How could they forget the seasonal sacrifices for dried provisions,
cut off the wine cups for fermented drinks!
If one is not perfectly self-sufficient,
how can one be considered free and unfettered!"
This is what Xiàng Guō's commentary did not fully explore.

[遙] as the character itself indicates.

◎Qìng Fān's note: The two characters 逍遙,
are not included in the Shuōwén dictionary;
it is correct to write them as 消搖.
In the Book of Rites, Tán Gōng chapter: "wandering idly at the door";
In the History of the Han Dynasty, Biography of Sīmǎ Xiàngrú: "wandering idly in Xiāng Yáng";
Jīng Shān quotes from the Classic of the Mystery, "Even if the united heads wish to be free and unfettered,
Heaven will not allow it";
On the stone pillars of the Kaìmǔ Shrine of the Hàn Dynasty, it is written: "Adorned with brilliance and freedom";
In the Selections of Literature, Sòng Yù's "Nine Arguments": "I will idly wander in contemplation";
In the History of the Later Hàn, Biography of Dōngpíng Xiàn Wáng Cāng: "wandering idly in contemplation";
The characters are all written with the water radical for 消,
and the hand radical for 搖.
In the Táng Dynasty, Buddhist monk Zhànrán's Auxiliary Conduct for the Cessation and Contemplation, Hóng Jué quotes Wáng Mào saying at night:
"消搖 means,
the idea of being harmoniously carefree and leisurely."
Indeed, perfect principle is sufficient within;
there is no time when it is not suitable;
focusing the mind on responding to things;
there is nowhere it does not penetrate.
By this, one travels the world;
therefore it is called 消搖.
Furthermore, it is said:
The principle (lǐ) has no hidden depths,
It vanishes yet is fitting,
Form has no great or small,
It sways yet is all-pervading,
therefore it is called *xiāo yáo*.
Explaining the meaning of *xiāo yáo*,
[Zhuāngzǐ] surpasses all scholars.
*Yóu* [遊] is as the character [is].
It is also written as *yóu* [游].
*Xiāo Yáo Yóu* [逍遙遊],
is the name of the chapter,
Its meaning is taken to be leisurely and unrestrained,
Cheerful and content.
◎ Qìng Fān observes: My late father, Minister of the Household, said:
In the *Tiān Xià* chapter, Zhuāngzǐ speaks of his doctrine and arts as substantial and inexhaustible,
and he roams above with the Creator.
The first chapter is entitled *Xiāo Yáo Yóu*,
Zhuāngzǐ uses its boundless words to describe himself.
The commentary says that although small and great are different,
*xiāo yáo* is the same [for both].
This seems to miss the point of Zhuāngzǐ.
◎ Furthermore, in the annotation to Pān Ānrén's "Autumn Excursion Ode" in the *Wén Xuǎn*, it quotes Sīmǎ Biāo saying:
Speaking of *xiāo yáo wú wéi*, it means being able to roam the Great Dao.

【Commentary】 *Míng*,
is similar to "sea,"
taking from it the boundless and limitless vastness,
therefore (called) [it is called] = "called" was often confused in ancient times,
now it is distinguished by meaning.
It will not appear again.
= of *Míng*.
*Dōngfāng Shuò*'s *Shí Zhōu Jì* says:
"The *Míng* sea has no wind, yet its vast waves are a hundred *zhàng* high."
Within this giant sea,
there is this large fish.
Intending to clarify that the nature of things is natural,
therefore it is marked as the chapter's beginning.
*Xuán Zhōng Jì* says:
"In the east, there is a large fish,
a traveler takes one day to pass its head,
and seven days to pass its tail;
during the three days of spawning,
the azure sea turns red because of it."
Therefore, know that large things are born in large places,
not only in the Northern Sea.

夫莊子之大意， The main idea of Zhuāngzǐ 莊子,
在乎逍遙遊放， Lies in carefree wandering and unrestrained freedom,
無為而自得， Achieving self-possession through non-action (wúwéi 無為),
故極小大之致以明性分之適。 Therefore, he exhausts the extremes of smallness and greatness to illuminate the suitability of inherent nature and allotted fate.

宜要其會歸而遺其所寄， Should grasp its ultimate meaning and disregard its allegorical vehicles.

@【疏】夫四序風馳， @ [Subcommentary:] The four seasons rush by like the wind,
三光電卷， The sun, moon, and stars unroll like lightning,
是以負山岳而捨故， Therefore, carrying mountains on their backs, they abandon the old,
揚舟壑以趨新。 And raising boats in ravines, they hasten toward the new.

欲明變化之大理也。 Intends to illuminate the great principle of transformation.
